title: The senior LLM system design interview
summary: Turn an ambiguous assistant request into a defensible architecture, quantified capacity plan, evaluation contract, and reversible deployment.
learningObjectives: Translate business requirements into workload, privacy, quality, and latency contracts.
Calculate input/output demand, average concurrency, failure headroom, and cost per successful task.
Choose hosting, retrieval, and adaptation independently and defend their tradeoffs.
Explain load testing, evaluation gates, deployment, and rollback as one coherent system.

sections.title: 1. Spend the interview on decisions
paragraphs: This article walks through a senior-level system design interview for an LLM product: the kind of question where an interviewer says "design an internal chat assistant for our company" and then pokes at every choice you make. Most of the building blocks (serving, the KV cache, retrieval, evaluation, security) have their own articles in this curriculum; here the focus is on stitching them together under time pressure. At the senior level, the interview mostly tests whether your assumptions lead to decisions that survive changed requirements. Begin with the user task and a measurable outcome, then draw the smallest system capable of producing it. Naming many frameworks is less useful than explaining why a boundary exists, what failure crosses it, and which measurement would invalidate your choice.

Time is the scarce resource in these interviews, so it helps to walk in with a rough plan. The figure at the end of this section lays out one possible 45-minute allocation; treat it as a negotiation with the interviewer rather than a script. Spend minutes 0–6 clarifying requirements, 6–12 estimating workload, 12–22 drawing architecture, 22–31 examining serving capacity and failures, 31–39 explaining evaluation and release controls, and 39–45 defending alternatives. State unresolved assumptions aloud and keep a short decision ledger (a running note of what you decided and why, so you can revisit it quickly). If the interviewer changes privacy or scale, revise the affected decisions instead of restarting the diagram. Reserve the final minute for the largest remaining uncertainty and the experiment that resolves it. The rest of this article follows that same order, using one example problem from start to finish.

sections.title: 2. Establish a concrete requirements contract
paragraphs: To keep things concrete, let's pick an example problem. Consider an internal policy assistant for 5,000 employees. It answers questions using current company documents, supplies supporting citations, and abstains when evidence is missing. It cannot approve expenses or change records. Assume 2 requests/second during ordinary busy periods and 8 requests/second during a ten-minute burst. User count alone cannot determine either rate: ask about active users, sessions, turns, geography, and synchronized events (say, everyone checking the new travel policy right after an all-hands meeting).

Next, pin down what "good" means with actual numbers. Propose explicit targets for discussion: 95% of valid requests receive a first answer token within 2 seconds (often called time to first token, the moment the reply starts streaming back), 95% finish within 15 seconds, and 99.5% complete without infrastructure failure over a rolling month. Define the eligible request population and count admission rejections (requests the system turns away because it is full) against availability when the contract promises capacity. A separate held-out assessment (a test set kept apart from anything you tuned on) requires at least 90% task success, with correctness, citation support, permission compliance, and appropriate abstention in its rubric. These are hypothetical requirements, not achieved results. Notice that quality, reliability, and data policy end up as three separate contracts; the figure at the end of this section puts them side by side, and passing one tells you little about the others.

The third contract is about data. Classify documents and prompts before choosing a provider. In this example, restricted content must stay on company infrastructure; approved public content may use an external API under a reviewed retention policy. Decide data residency (which region the data physically lives in), deletion, log access, and who can inspect traces. Permission leakage is a release-blocking failure, not a small average-quality penalty. Google SRE's guidance on service level objectives (SLOs, explicit reliability targets like the ones above) motivates user-centered indicators and explicit measurement windows; the particular targets here are design assumptions.

diagram.title: Three independent acceptance contracts
diagram.caption: Passing one contract does not imply passing the others.

nodes.label: Service reliability

sections.title: 3. Translate requests into two token workloads
paragraphs: With the requirements written down, the next step is turning requests into tokens, since tokens are what the model actually reads and writes (the Inside a decoder: from text to the next token article covers where they come from). Budget the entire model input: 500 system and tool-schema tokens, 300 question tokens, 1,200 history tokens, and 2,000 retrieved-context tokens give an illustrative mean of 4,000 input tokens. The bar chart at the end of this section shows how those four pieces stack up. Assume 400 generated tokens on average, with a 600-token output limit and a separate maximum input limit. Count with the selected tokenizer and include repeated prompts in multi-call workflows. Input plus reserved output must fit the model's usable context window (the maximum number of tokens it can handle in one request).

Now multiply by traffic. Using the arrival rate (written λ in the formula box below) at the 8-request/second burst, demand is 32,000 input tokens/second and 3,200 output tokens/second. These are separate capacity requirements: prefill processes the whole input context in one large parallel pass, while autoregressive decode produces output incrementally, one token at a time, each step depending on the last. A rough analogy: prefill is reading the question, decode is writing the answer word by word, and they stress the hardware in different ways (the Serving LLMs: KV Cache as a Memory and Latency Budget article goes deeper). They compete for shared resources in many deployments. Do not add their rates and compare the result to a single advertised throughput number. Cached prefixes (reusing the computed work for a repeated prompt start, such as the system instructions) may reduce repeated computation, but cold-cache failover, where a backup replica starts without any of that cached work, must remain feasible.

The last workload question is how many requests are in flight at once. Suppose mean end-to-end residence time, including queueing, retrieval, and generation, is 10 seconds at this load. Little's law, a queueing rule stating that the average number of items in a system equals arrival rate times average time spent inside (L = λW), gives 80 requests in the whole system on average. Think of a coffee shop: if eight customers walk in every second and each stays ten seconds, you'd expect about 80 people inside at any moment. It requires a stable population and consistent boundaries; it does not prove that 80 GPU sequences suffice, and multiplying peak arrivals by p95 latency (the latency 95% of requests beat) does not yield p95 concurrency. Measure service-stage concurrency, prompt-length tails, and KV-cache occupancy (GPU memory holding each active request's attention state) separately. With 400 output tokens and 2 seconds to first token, a 10-second completion assumption implies roughly 50 output tokens/second per active stream, which must be validated under concurrent load. The formula box below collects all three calculations.
sections.formula: Input demand = λ × E[P] = 8 requests/s × 4,000 tokens/request = 32,000 tokens/s; output demand = λ × E[O] = 3,200 tokens/s; L = λW = 8 requests/s × 10 s = 80 requests

sections.title: 4. Choose hosting, knowledge, and behavior separately
paragraphs: With the workload sized, you can start choosing components. One thing that helps is noticing that several choices are independent of each other (the figure at the end of this section lays out the three axes). Local hosting versus an API is a deployment decision. Retrieval versus fine-tuning is a knowledge and behavior decision. They are not four mutually exclusive architectures. Start this example with a local instruction model (a model tuned to follow instructions, running on company hardware) plus retrieval because restricted documents cannot leave the company and policies change frequently. Compare an approved API on the public-data evaluation slice when its quality or operational convenience may justify the cost.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means the system looks up relevant documents and hands them to the model alongside the question; the RAG: Retrieving Evidence Before Generating Answers article covers it in detail. It works a bit like an open-book exam: the model doesn't need to memorize the policy manual if it can look up the right page. The RAG paper establishes the combination of parametric model knowledge (what is baked into the weights) with external retrieved memory. In this design, ingestion preserves document versions and access metadata, retrieval applies user permissions, and generation cites the selected evidence. Retrieval can fail through missing coverage, stale indexing, poor ranking, or malicious document instructions (prompt injection, discussed in the LLM Security article). Evaluate those stages independently before blaming the model. Retrieved text supplies evidence; it does not acquire authority to change system rules.

Fine-tuning becomes plausible when representative labeled examples reveal a recurring behavior problem, such as inconsistent extraction format, after prompt and retrieval improvements. LoRA (covered in the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning article) trains small low-rank update matrices while freezing base weights; reduced trainable parameters do not remove data preparation, evaluation, or serving compatibility costs. It is not a substitute for authorization or fresh facts. Pretraining a new model would require a distinct capability and data argument, not merely dissatisfaction with a prototype.

diagram.title: Independent design axes
diagram.caption: Choose one or more options on each axis using task evidence and constraints.

nodes.detail: Local: data control and operations burden. API: managed capacity with provider, retention, and quota constraints.

nodes.label: Knowledge
nodes.detail: Retrieval: versioned external evidence and permissions. Context-only: simpler when all necessary material already fits.

sections.title: 5. Draw ownership and failure boundaries
paragraphs: Next, draw the request path and say who owns what at each box. The curriculum's educational farm (from the Designing a two-server corporate Qwen farm article) makes a handy reference: browser to Nginx gateway (the front door that terminates TLS and spreads traffic), then stateless Express replicas (Node.js API servers that keep no per-user state in memory), then either of two same-model inference endpoints. Express owns authentication, conversation authorization, request identifiers, provider policy, and Postgres writes. Postgres owns durable history and revision state. Inference hosts own computation and ephemeral caches. This is a conceptual Linux deployment example, not a claim that the Windows learning application runs an inference cluster. The figure at the end of this section follows one request through these boundaries.

Persist the user turn before generation and finalize the assistant turn as complete, error, or canceled. Use expected revisions (the client states which version of the conversation it is building on, so conflicting writes get caught) and idempotency keys (a unique ID per send, so a retry doesn't create a second copy) to prevent accidental duplicate turns, without holding a database transaction throughout generation. Server-Sent Events (SSE), a simple HTTP streaming format, deliver interactive output; once tokens are visible, silently restarting generation risks contradictory answers. Report the partial result and let the client reconcile against authoritative history. A bounded pre-output retry may be permissible within the remaining deadline.

Nginx least-connection balancing (sending each request to the replica with the fewest open connections) suits stateless API replicas. Optional conversation-based rendezvous placement among healthy same-model inference hosts, a hashing scheme that keeps sending a conversation to the same host, can improve cache locality (the Routing a Local AI Farm Without Losing Conversation Truth article covers it); it does not establish conversation correctness. Failover loses that warmth, since the new host starts with a cold cache. Do not introduce Kafka (a durable message log) merely to connect chat to inference. Durable asynchronous tasks need an outbox or queue, leases, idempotency, and ordering, which solve a different delivery problem. Any future agent tools also need scoped credentials and explicit side-effect boundaries.

sections.title: 6. Buy capacity that still works after a failure
paragraphs: Once the path is drawn, a likely follow-up is "how many machines do you need?" Suppose a future benchmark demonstrates that one replica sustains this exact request mix at 2 requests/second while meeting both latency targets. Treat that number as a hypothetical sizing input, not a measured model benchmark. If four surviving replicas must serve 8 requests/second, five replicas provide single-replica failure coverage but leave the survivors at their tested ceiling. Six replicas leave five after a failure, placing them at 80% of that ceiling. The formula box below writes this out, and the figure at the end of the section compares the four, five, and six replica options. The appropriate margin depends on variability, recovery time, and the capacity of shared dependencies.

It helps to be precise about what a replica is. A replica is a complete serving unit, potentially spanning multiple GPUs. Estimate weight memory, KV memory for active sequences, runtime buffers, and fragmentation before selecting hardware. Tensor parallelism (splitting each layer across several GPUs) may make a model fit while adding communication costs; data parallelism (running more full copies) adds independent serving capacity. The Mixture of Experts and Parallelism article covers both. Quantization (storing weights in fewer bits, see the Quantization and Compression article) may improve fit but needs quality and kernel-performance validation. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model only uses some of its parameters for each token, but all of them still have to sit in memory, so MoE's active parameters do not describe its entire memory footprint. Efficient attention and continuous batching (adding new requests to a running batch as others finish, covered in the Inference Scheduling article) help different bottlenecks and cannot rescue unbounded admission, where every request is let in no matter how full the system is.

Numbers on paper still need a load test to back them up. Load-test realistic joint distributions of input lengths, output lengths, arrival bursts, and cache reuse. Use open-loop arrival tests, where requests arrive on a fixed schedule rather than waiting for earlier responses, so slow responses do not automatically reduce offered demand and hide overload. Include cold starts, one lost replica, slow retrieval, database pressure, cancellations, and provider throttling. Record successful SLO-compliant throughput, rejection rate, queue time, first-token latency, per-request decode speed, and memory pressure. vLLM, a popular open-source inference server, documents separate request-level and streamed-output latency metrics; preserve their different aggregation semantics.
sections.formula: Failure utilization = λpeak / ((N − f) × r); with λpeak = 8 requests/s, N = 6, f = 1, r = 2 requests/s: utilization = 8/10 = 80%

diagram.title: Illustrative replica headroom
diagram.caption: Assumes identical replicas hypothetically validated at 2 requests/second for this workload. Shared bottlenecks can invalidate this arithmetic.

sections.title: 7. Price successful tasks and bounded failure
paragraphs: Capacity costs money, which leads to another question interviewers like to ask: is this design worth what it costs? A useful framing is to optimize cost per successful task, not the cheapest token. Include inference, idle reserved capacity, retrieval, storage, networking, retries, operational work, and human review over the same accounting window. Define success consistently across candidates. If a hypothetical system costs 240 currency units for 1,000 attempted tasks and succeeds on 800, its cost is 0.30 per success. A second costs 200 but succeeds on 500, giving 0.40 per success, so the cheaper system is actually more expensive per useful answer. These invented accounting examples are not vendor prices. The formula box below states the ratio, and the steps at the end of this section outline a fair comparison.

A cascade (a chain of models tried cheapest first) can route easy tasks to a smaller model and difficult tasks to a stronger approved model, a bit like a help desk where tier one handles routine tickets and escalates the hard ones. Routing errors and second attempts consume both latency and money, though. Estimate escalation rates using held-out traffic. Bound queue length, tool steps, generated tokens, and retry budgets. Deadline propagation (passing the remaining time budget to every downstream call), backoff, and jitter (random spread in retry timing so clients don't retry in lockstep) reduce uncontrolled retry amplification, as explained by the AWS Builders' Library. Overload should produce explicit HTTP 429 (too many requests) or 503 (service unavailable) responses, not endless waiting. Restricted requests must never fail over to a forbidden provider.
sections.formula: Cost per successful task = total attributable cost in window / successful tasks in the same window

sections.title: 8. Make quality releases reversible
paragraphs: The last stretch of the interview is usually about shipping changes safely, since a new model or prompt can quietly hurt quality without throwing a single error. Build a versioned evaluation set spanning common questions, rare policies, missing evidence, conflicting revisions, long histories, and adversarial instructions. Keep development examples separate from final assessment and inspect slices rather than only averages. Use deterministic checks for schema and citation existence, expert review for support and correctness, and calibrated model judges (another LLM grading outputs, checked against human labels; see the Evaluation and Observability article) where useful. NIST's generative-AI risk profile supplies a broad risk-management reference; this specific evaluation design remains a proposal to validate with stakeholders.

Version model weights, tokenizer, prompt template, retrieval index, permissions logic, and decoding settings (temperature and similar sampling parameters) as a release bundle. Shadow evaluation (running the new bundle on copies of real traffic without showing users its output) must obey the same privacy policy as production. Canary a small eligible cohort, meaning you release to a small slice of users first (named after the canaries miners once used as an early warning), watch latency and quality signals, and stop expansion on predefined regression gates. Roll back the bundle coherently; restoring an old index must not restore revoked permissions. Keep the previous compatible bundle available and rehearse rollback. Delayed human quality labels require slower promotion than immediate infrastructure metrics alone would suggest. The figure at the end of this section traces this release path gate by gate.

To close out, defend the architecture by naming what would change your mind. Poor retrieval recall suggests indexing or ranking work; good evidence with consistently wrong answers suggests model or adaptation work; high first-token delay with stable decode suggests queueing or prefill investigation. If a smaller quantized model passes the task rubric, it may improve economics; if it fails critical slices, memory savings are irrelevant. A strong closing answer ties model fundamentals, data quality, adaptation, serving, security, and operations to the same user outcome.

diagram.caption: A release is a versioned system bundle; each gate can stop promotion.

interview.question: Design the internal policy assistant above in 45 minutes. The interviewer then doubles average retrieved context and says one inference host must be removable during working hours. What changes?
interview.answer: First preserve the requirements contract and clarify whether the doubled context improves measured answer quality. Mean input grows from 4,000 to 6,000 tokens because only the 2,000-token retrieval component doubles. Peak input demand becomes 48,000 tokens/second while assumed output demand remains 3,200. Rebenchmark prefill, first-token latency, KV occupancy, and concurrency; the previous replica throughput is no longer valid. Test evidence compression or reranking against the quality rubric rather than truncating blindly. Capacity must meet the declared burst with one host absent, accounting for how many complete replicas that host contains. Keep bounded admission, explicit partial-generation status, and privacy-safe routing. Promote a new configuration only after quality, realistic load, and failure tests pass, with a compatible rollback bundle ready.
followUps: How would a three-call agent workflow change demand and successful-task accounting?
Which observations distinguish retrieval failure from generator failure?
Why does doubling replica count not guarantee halved latency?
What if cloud APIs outperform the local model on restricted questions?
How do you preserve document revocations when rolling back an index?

pitfalls: Inferring request rate from registered user count without a usage model.
Using average prompt length to justify an unrestricted maximum context.
Multiplying peak arrival rate by p95 latency and calling the result p95 concurrency.
Treating local/API and RAG/fine-tuning as mutually exclusive choices.
Claiming a capacity estimate is a measured benchmark.
Letting cache affinity become the source of conversation correctness.
Counting HTTP success as semantic task success.
Retrying a visible partial generation silently or routing private data to an unapproved fallback.
checklist: Write the user task, exclusions, data boundary, and success rubric before selecting models.
State arrival and token distributions, burst duration, and context/output limits.
Compute input and output rates separately and apply Little's law to a named boundary.
Draw durable state ownership and permission enforcement on the request path.
Measure the chosen workload at target latency before sizing failure headroom.
Test cold caches, replica loss, dependency slowness, and open-loop overload.
Compare total cost per successful task using a consistent denominator.
Define release gates, coherent versioning, and a rehearsed rollback that preserves revocations.

flashcards.front: What should precede a model choice in a system design interview?
flashcards.back: A task and acceptance contract: workload, data boundaries, quality, latency, and failure behavior. These determine which candidates are feasible and what evidence can compare them.

flashcards.front: Why estimate input and output tokens/second separately?
flashcards.back: Prefill and autoregressive decode have different execution patterns and resource demands. A single aggregate rate hides which phase limits the workload.

flashcards.front: At 8 requests/second and 10 seconds mean residence time, what does Little's law imply?
flashcards.back: 80 requests in the named system on average under stable conditions. It does not imply 80 GPU sequences or a tail concurrency percentile.

flashcards.front: Which tokens belong in the input budget?
flashcards.back: System instructions, tool schemas, current input, conversation history, retrieved evidence, and other serialized context. Reserving output space prevents accidental context overflow.

flashcards.front: Why are local hosting, APIs, RAG, and fine-tuning not four exclusive alternatives?
flashcards.back: Hosting selects where computation occurs; retrieval supplies external knowledge; fine-tuning changes behavior. A locally hosted fine-tuned model can also use retrieval.

flashcards.front: Why choose retrieval for changing company policies?
flashcards.back: Versioned external evidence can be updated and authorized independently of model weights. Retrieval still requires recall, freshness, permission, and grounding evaluation.

flashcards.front: When is LoRA a defensible next step?
flashcards.back: When representative labeled failures show a stable behavior gap that simpler changes did not resolve. Training fewer parameters does not eliminate data quality or regression evaluation needs.

flashcards.front: What is failure utilization for six 2-request/second replicas serving 8 requests/second with one lost?
flashcards.back: 8 divided by five surviving replicas times 2 equals 80%. This depends on validated per-replica capacity and absence of a shared bottleneck.
They keep offered arrivals independent of response completion. Closed-loop clients can slow their arrivals when the service slows, hiding the severity of overload.

flashcards.front: Why compare cost per successful task?
flashcards.back: Cheap attempts can require retries or fail more often. Total attributable cost divided by consistent task successes captures that economic effect better than token price alone.

flashcards.front: Why is inference cache locality not conversation consistency?
flashcards.back: Caches are disposable performance state. Durable turns, authorization, revisions, and idempotency live in the application and database so correctness survives inference failover.

flashcards.front: What changes after generation tokens have reached a client?
flashcards.back: A silent retry could produce a different continuation or duplicate answer. Expose a partial/error state and reconcile authoritative history instead of pretending the request never started.

flashcards.front: What belongs in an LLM release bundle?
flashcards.back: Model, tokenizer, prompt, retrieval index, decoding configuration, and compatible application behavior. Coordinated versioning enables meaningful attribution and rollback while current permissions remain enforced.

flashcards.front: What makes a tradeoff defense senior-level?
flashcards.back: State the constraint, decision, evidence, downside, and condition that would change the decision. This shows the design is testable rather than loyalty to a model or framework.
